t.7.18.1: When Vedavatī had entered the fire, Rāvaṇa mounted that Puṣpaka and roamed all over the earth.
t.7.18.2: Then, having reached Uśīrabīja, that Rākṣasa beheld King Marutta performing a sacrifice together with the gods.
t.7.18.3: The brahmarṣi named Saṃvarta, the very brother of Bṛhaspati, a knower of dharma, surrounded by all the hosts of brahmins, conducted the sacrifice.
t.7.18.4: But the gods, seeing that Rākṣasa rendered invincible by the granting of a boon, and fearing an assault from him, took on various animal forms.
t.7.18.5: Indra became a peacock, while Dharmarāja became a crow; the Lord of Wealth became a lizard, and Varuṇa became a swan.
t.7.18.6: And having approached that king, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, said: "Give me battle, or else say, 'I am conquered.'"
t.7.18.7: Then King Marutta said to him, "Who are you?" Thereupon the rākṣasa, letting out a burst of mocking laughter, spoke these words.
t.7.18.8: I am pleased, O king, with your lack of curiosity, you who do not recognize me as Rāvaṇa, the younger brother of Dhanada.
t.7.18.9: Who is there in the three worlds who does not know my strength, the strength by which, having conquered my brother, this aerial chariot was carried off?
t.7.18.10: Then King Marutta said to that Rākṣasa: "Fortunate indeed are you, by whom your elder brother was conquered in battle!"
t.7.18.11: A deed joined with unrighteousness is not praiseworthy, nor is one the world condemns; yet having done a wicked deed, you boast of conquering your brother.
t.7.18.12: Did you obtain your boon only after practising nothing but dharma beforehand? For I have never before heard of such a thing as you yourself are describing.
t.7.18.13: Then the king, enraged, took up his bow and arrows and set out for battle, but Saṃvarta barred his way.
t.7.18.14: That great sage spoke to Marutta words filled with affection: "If my word is to be heeded, a battle is not fitting for you."
t.7.18.15: This sacrifice to Maheśvara, if left unfinished, would burn up my whole family. How can one who is consecrated for a sacrifice wage war? How can there be cruelty in one who is consecrated?
t.7.18.16: "The outcome in battle is ever uncertain, and this rākṣasa is hard to conquer." Turned back by his guru's words, Marutta, lord of the earth, laid down his bow together with its arrows and, composed once more, turned his face toward the sacrifice.
t.7.18.18: Having devoured those great sages who were there, having come to the sacrifice, and fully sated with their blood, he set out once more across the earth.
t.7.18.17: Then, deeming him defeated, Śuka proclaimed, "Rāvaṇa has conquered!" and out of joy he let forth a roar.
t.7.18.19: When Rāvaṇa had gone, the gods, the dwellers of heaven together with Indra, returned to their own forms and then spoke to those creatures.
t.7.18.20: Then Indra, out of joy, said to the blue-plumed peacock: "O bird, I, who know dharma, am pleased with you because of the help you gave."
t.7.18.21: The thousand eyes that are mine shall be on your tail-feathers. When I pour down rain, you shall attain joy, the very sign of delight.
t.7.18.22: Formerly, they say, O lord of men, the tail feathers of peacocks were blue; but having received a boon from the lord of the gods, they all became many-hued.
t.7.18.23: O Rāma, Dharmarāja spoke to the crow perched on the eastern beam of the sacrificial hall: “O bird, I am well pleased with you; now hear the words of one who is pleased.”
t.7.18.24: Other living beings are afflicted by me with various diseases, but those diseases will have no power over you, since I am pleased with you; of this there is no doubt.
t.7.18.25: By virtue of my boons, O bird, you shall have no fear of death; as long as men do not kill you, so long shall you live.
t.7.18.26: And those men dwelling in my realm who are tormented by hunger will be satisfied, together with their kinsmen, once you have eaten.
t.7.18.28: Your color shall be charming and gentle, like the orb of the moon, surpassingly bright, shining with a radiance equal to white foam.
t.7.18.27: Varuṇa then spoke to the swan that moved upon the waters of the Gaṅgā: "Hear these words full of affection, O lord of the winged ones."
t.7.18.29: Having taken on my bodily form, you will be lovely forever, and you will obtain incomparable joy; this is the token of my affection.
t.7.18.30: For in former times, O Rāma, the colour of swans was not wholly white; their wings were tipped with dark blue, and their breasts were as clear as the tips of tender young grass.
t.7.18.31: Then Vaiśravaṇa said to the chameleon standing on the mountain: "I bestow upon you a golden colour, for I too am pleased with you."
t.7.18.32: Your head shall forever be endowed with wealth and shall be imperishable, and through my favor this golden hue shall be yours.
t.7.18.33: Having thus granted boons to them, the gods, when that sacrificial festival had come to an end, went back again together with the king to their own abode.
